description.narrative: BankWiser International is a project that organises and aims to create additional civil soceity capacity in 11 countries, whereof four are DAC countries, to evaluate and monitor major commenrcial banks' CSR policies and practices and to mobilise bank clients to request a more responsible banking sector.
BankWiser avser att öka tillgängligheten för bankkunder till finansiella intitutioners CSR strategier och CSR genomförande och att påverka banksektorn att ta ett ökat CSR ansvar.

Fair Finance Guide avser att öka tillgängligheten för bankkunder till finansiella intitutioners hållbarhets strategier och genomförande. Syfte med insatser är att påverka banksektorn att ta ett ökat hållbarhets ansvar.

sector.narrative: Education/training in banking and financial services

description.narrative: The Fair Finance Guide International (FFGI) project started in 2014 as the Bankwiser International Project, and changed its name in 2015. Within the framework of the project, 3 years, a network of 9 CSO coalitions in 9 countries were created. Each coalition assessed the policies and practices of banks and uses the research outcomes to inform the bank clients who then demanded more responsible behaviour of their banks; and influenced the banks directly and/or through engagement of regulators and financial authorities. Within the FFGI network, the coalitions developed a joint bank policy assessment methodology and joint communication and campaign tools; furthermore, they worked together on joint research and influencing, exchanged data and designed, and learnt from each other’s experiences. As a global coalition, the FFGI is in its early stages of development, growing from one country at the start of the programme in 2014 (The Netherlands, where a FFG assessment – the ‘Eerlijke Bankwijzer’ – is being published since 2009) to at least nine in 2017. The expansion from a national initiative to an international one has largely been financed by Sida, coupled with Oxfam Novib and its partners own contribution. Relative to the time spent on developing the network if compared to other global networks, relative to the complexity of the market in which it operates and also relative to its initial programme goals, the FFGI has been an unequivocal success so far. Part of this success is due to the fact that as the expansion was undertaken, The Netherlands already had 6 years of experience and had developed a solid methodology and theory of change on which others could build. Furthermore, the FFG’s has built on existing initiatives and expertise of CSOs and individuals in other coalition countries.
